name: Rhenish salt-glaze stoneware
region: Siegburg, Raeren, Cologne, Frechen and the Westerwald, Rhineland
summary: Hard grey stoneware that the potters of the Rhineland fired to about 1250 °C and glazed with salt. The jugs, bottles and storage jars are tough, waterproof and ready for the cellar.

philosophy.core_thesis: A dense stoneware pot needs no lining, because a handful of salt thrown into the hot kiln gives it a skin that keeps out water and does not taste of lead.
design_principles: Throw the body of a local stoneware clay and fire it to 1200 to 1300 °C until it does not take up water.
Throw rock salt into the firebox at the peak of the firing; the vapour forms a glaze 0.1 mm thick with an orange-peel texture.
Press a face mask, a coat of arms or a rosette in relief on the neck or the belly of a jug.
Keep the neck narrow and the belly round, so that the jug holds 1 to 5 litres and pours well.
Pull a strap handle and fix it with slip at the neck and at the belly.
Colour the surface in the fire: tan to brown with iron in the clay; after 1590 add cobalt blue and manganese purple in the Westerwald.
Stack the pots in the kiln with a gap of 2 to 3 cm, so that the salt vapour reaches every face.
anti_patterns: A smooth, glossy, even glaze with no texture
A white or cream body that shows through the glaze
Thin printed lines with no relief
Bright overglaze colours on the surface

form.shape: Bartmann jugs with a bearded face on the neck, round-bellied bottles, tall storage jars, cylindrical tankards and wide mugs.
form.profile: A narrow neck on a round belly that swells to the lower third; the body narrows to a flat base.
form.foot_and_rim: A flat base cut off the wheel with wire, with a frilled or pinched foot in some Siegburg work; a plain rolled rim with a lip for the pour.
form.proportion: Height 15 to 40 cm; the wall is 4 to 7 mm thick, which is thin for stoneware.
rules: Put the face mask on the neck of a jug, and let the beard fall to the shoulder.
Keep the belly round and the handle a simple strap.
Leave the base unglazed or lightly salted.

bodies.rule: Use a plastic grey or white-burning clay that vitrifies at 1200 °C. Keep earthenware and porcelain out: a salt glaze only forms on a dense, silica-rich stoneware. Silver is only for lids and mounts.

methods: press moulding of relief masks and medallions
forming.joins: Handles are luted with slip at the neck and the belly; sprigs are pressed on a wet face and smoothed at the edge.
forming.details: Throwing rings on the belly, a thin clay slip wash on the neck, and an orange-peel skin where the salt vapour settled.

glaze.pattern: Bearded face masks, coats of arms, rosettes and oak-leaf medallions in relief; in the Westerwald, incised scrolls filled with cobalt blue and manganese purple.
glaze.gloss: A semi-gloss skin of about 20 to 45 GU, with an orange-peel texture.
glaze.wear: The salt skin is hard and does not chip; the colour of the body shows grey, tan or brown at the foot.

palette.strategy: Earth colours from the fire: grey, tan and iron brown, with Westerwald cobalt blue and manganese purple as the only strong accents.

firing.kiln: A wood-fired kiln of 2 to 4 cubic metres; rock salt is thrown in through ports in the wall.
processes: bisque-dry the pots in the open air
stack the pots in the kiln
throw rock salt through the ports
close the kiln and let it cool for 2 days
firing.scale: By 1500 more than 100 potters worked in Siegburg and Raeren; Frechen jugs went to London and the Low Countries by the barrel.
firing.signs: Orange-peel texture, a darker brown flash where the salt hit the wall, and a dry unglazed base.

lineage.root: Rhineland potters fired the first salt-glazed stoneware; no earlier style in this data leads to it.

emotion.target_response: A sturdy, earthy calm: the viewer feels the weight of a pot that has held beer, wine and oil for 400 years.

use_cases: a period prompt for a cellar, a tavern or a kitchen of the 16th century
a museum label on German stoneware
a brief for a rustic jug with relief and salt glaze
avoid_when: the brief needs a smooth gloss glaze
the brief needs a white body
the brief is for translucent tableware

modifiers.how: Change the body to earthenware, cover it with a white tin glaze and paint the pattern in cobalt.
Make the form a straight-sided crock, use a brown slip or salt glaze and paint one cobalt motif.

wall_thickness.note: Stoneware holds a thin wall; a Bartmann jug is thinner than earthenware of the same size.
